intro: For more than two thousand years, students across China, Korea, Japan and Vietnam learned from the same small library. It held the Five Classics and, later, the Four Books. Officials had to know them. Poets quoted them. Families argued over them at dinner.

In this unit you will open that library. You will learn what each of the Five Classics is and how Zhu Xi built the Four Books. You will look inside the Analects to see how it was put together. Then you will follow a great debate inside the Confucian tradition: Mencius and Xunzi on whether human nature is good.

By the end, you will be able to name the classics and their genres, read a citation like Mencius 2A.6, and explain both sides of the human nature debate. You will use the words of the texts themselves as your evidence.
bigQuestion: What did the Confucian classics teach, and why did their readers argue about them?

timeline.t: Earliest poems of the Book of Songs (c. 1000–600 BCE)
Confucius dies (traditional date); students begin gathering his sayings
Han court creates posts for scholars of the Five Classics
Zhu Xi publishes the Four Books with his commentary
Zhu Xi's commentary becomes the standard for the exams
Joseon Korea begins; Zhu Xi's learning becomes official there
James Legge publishes the Analects in English (2nd ed. 1893)
China ends the exams on the classics

test.q: Which book is one of the Five Classics?
test.why: The Book of Changes (Yijing) is one of the Five Classics.

test.q: How many poems are in the Book of Songs?

test.why: Zhu Xi grouped them and published his commentary in 1190.

test.q: The Great Learning and Doctrine of the Mean were first chapters of which book?
test.why: Both were chapters of the Liji, the Book of Rites.

test.q: How do scholars describe the making of the Analects?
choices: Gathered by students over time, perhaps in layers
test.why: The Analects was compiled by students and later followers, and scholars debate its layers.

test.q: What does Analects book 10 mainly describe?
test.why: Book 10 describes how Confucius behaved at court, home and meals.

test.q: Why could scholars in Korea, Japan and Vietnam read the classics?
test.why: Classical Chinese served as a shared written language across East Asia.

test.q: What does Mencius 2A.6 use to show that people have compassion?
choices: A child about to fall into a well
test.why: Mencius uses the child at the well as a thought experiment.

test.q: Compassion is the sprout of which virtue, for Mencius?
test.why: Mencius names compassion as the beginning of ren.

choices: Human nature is bad; goodness comes from effort
Nature is neither good nor bad
test.why: Xunzi ch. 23 argues human nature is bad and goodness comes from conscious effort.

choices: Warped wood straightened in a press
test.why: Xunzi compares moral training to straightening warped wood.

test.q: In Mencius 6A.2, what does water flowing down stand for?
test.why: Mencius says nature tends to good as water flows downward.

test.q: What does Mencius rank lightest in 7B.14?
test.why: Mencius says the sovereign is the lightest.

test.q: In Mencius 1B.8, why is killing the tyrant Zhou not killing a ruler?
choices: A cruel ruler is only a 'fellow,' not a true ruler
test.why: Mencius says a ruler who destroys humaneness and rightness is only a fellow.

test.q: Which thinker became part of the Four Books?
test.why: Zhu Xi included the Mencius among the Four Books; Xunzi was left out.

write.prompt: Is human nature good? Explain how Mencius and Xunzi answer. Cite Mencius 2A.6 and 6A.2 (Legge, 1895) and Xunzi ch. 23 (paraphrased), and describe how Zhu Xi and later readers took sides or kept both.
tips: Cite each passage with its book and number, like Mencius 2A.6.
Attribute every view: "Mencius argued..." or "Xunzi claimed..."
Explain each image, such as the sprout or the warped board.
Compare the two thinkers rather than naming a winner.
Use unit words like human nature, four sprouts and conscious effort.
